answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the Cosmos DB account resource).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create: az cosmosdb create --name myDocDbAccount --resource-group myRG --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2 --enable-multiple-write-locations false

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (AzureRM provider): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "..." resource_group_name = "..." location = "..." offer_type = "Standard" }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: MongoDB-style connection string. Example: mongodb://username%40myAccount:password@myAccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&authSource=admin&retrywrites=false. (Note username typically includes '@<accountName>' and TLS/SSL=true is required; port commonly 10255 for TLS connections.)

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is billed in Cosmos DB RUs (Request Units). You provision RU/s (or use autoscale RUs) or use the Cosmos DB serverless option where available. It is not billed as plain vCores for the MongoDB API; throughput is RU-based.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Data-plane access for the MongoDB API is done with database users (SCRAM username/password) created on the account; management operations use Azure AD. There is no standard MongoDB-driver integration for Microsoft Entra ID tokens for data-plane auth — drivers authenticate with the DB username/password (the username often formatted as user@account). Azure AD (Entra) is used for Azure management APIs and RBAC to manage the account, not as a direct MongoDB auth mechanism in typical setups.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use standard MongoDB client drivers (e.g., mongodb or mongoose for Node.js). There is no separate, service-specific MongoDB driver — applications use the official MongoDB ecosystem libraries against the Azure Cosmos DB (MongoDB API) endpoint.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: As far as I know the Azure Cosmos DB MongoDB API does not expose MongoDB-native vector-index types (like a built-in 'vector' index) via createIndex. There is no standard createIndex syntax for DiskANN/HNSW/IVF in Cosmos DB's MongoDB endpoint (so I would not rely on a MongoDB createIndex({embedding: 'vector'}) command).

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text/hybrid search is typically implemented by integrating Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search (index Cosmos data into Azure Search) or by running and indexing data in a separate search service. Cosmos DB (MongoDB API) does not provide an Atlas-Search-like integrated full-text engine; use Azure Cognitive Search or an external search solution.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB's MongoDB API implements a subset of MongoDB’s wire protocol and historically tracks a limited set of server versions (commonly older versions like 3.6/4.0/4.2/4.4 depending on account configuration). Many MongoDB features are restricted or altered (server-side JavaScript, some aggregation stages, certain index types, and some admin commands are not supported). Expect a subset compatibility; test your exact MongoDB feature (transactions, change streams, certain operators) against the target account version.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: Use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator for local development (Microsoft's emulator). There is a Docker image (mcr.microsoft.com/cosmosdb/linux/azure-cosmos-emulator) for Linux. The MongoDB endpoint in Cosmos typically uses port 10255 for TLS in the cloud; the emulator exposes its endpoints on emulator-specific ports (check emulator docs), so for MongoDB-style testing use the emulator container and its displayed MongoDB port (commonly 10255 / mapped port).

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB provides a Change Feed (its native change-tracking mechanism). The MongoDB-style change stream API support has been limited historically. If you need change notifications use Cosmos DB Change Feed (enabled by default on containers) or validate whether the target MongoDB API version on your account exposes change streams. For Change Feed you typically consume via the Change Feed Processor or Azure Functions.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server profile for data-plane inspection tools targeted at Cosmos DB / DocumentDB. The general Azure MCP server can cover management-plane actions, but the documentdb-specific MCP server provides data-plane helpers (index inspection, explain plans) for this service.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name of Microsoft's managed document database service; it evolved into Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB became the SQL API). The Azure "DocumentDB" name predates and is distinct from other projects/services named DocumentDB (and is not the same as AWS DocumentDB). Azure Cosmos DB is Microsoft’s globally distributed multimodel database; the Cosmos MongoDB API is a compatibility layer that implements the MongoDB wire protocol on top of Cosmos DB's engine.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath is Microsoft’s proprietary Cosmos DB engine (not the upstream MongoDB server). It implements the MongoDB wire protocol for compatibility, so application code usually uses MongoDB drivers unchanged but you must account for Cosmos-specific limits and differences (throughput/RU model, supported aggregation stages, index semantics, and any unsupported commands).

answers.question: What index definition does this sample need for the loyalty ledger?
answers.answer: Create indexes on { accountId: 1, timestamp: -1 } for fast history queries and on { accountId: 1 } and { lifetimePoints: -1 } (or a compound index { accountId:1, lifetimePoints:-1 }) to support aggregation and tier calculations. Use createIndex({ accountId: 1, timestamp: -1 }) via the MongoDB driver.

answers.question: What transactional constraints must the sample respect to make multi-document transactions work in Cosmos DB MongoDB API?
answers.answer: Transactions require a session and are limited to documents in the same logical partition key (or same shard). To ensure atomic append-and-balance updates, store events and balance in documents that share the same partition key (e.g., accountId) and use startSession()/startTransaction() in the MongoDB driver before performing the updates.

answers.question: What connection options and driver settings should the Node.js sample use when connecting to the cluster?
answers.answer: Use mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, ssl: true, sslValidate: true, replicaSet: 'globaldb', authSource: 'admin' }) (adjust options to match the DOCUMENTDB_URI). Do not log the raw URI; read from env at runtime.

answers.question: What aggregation computes tier status from lifetime points?
answers.answer: Aggregation pipeline: [ { $match: { accountId: <id> } }, { $group: { _id: '$accountId', lifetimePoints: { $sum: '$points' } } }, { $project: { lifetimePoints: 1, tier: { $switch: { branches: [ { case: { $gte: ['$lifetimePoints', 100000] }, then: 'Platinum' }, { case: { $gte: ['$lifetimePoints', 50000] }, then: 'Gold' }, { case: { $gte: ['$lifetimePoints', 10000] }, then: 'Silver' } ], default: 'Bronze' } } } ]

answers.question: How will the sample read the connection string at runtime and what dev-time placeholder should it ship?
answers.answer: At runtime read the MongoDB URI from process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI. In the repo provide a .env.example with: DOCUMENTDB_URI='mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&authSource=admin' (placeholder only — never commit real credentials).
